hook: The witty voice of the Enlightenment, who fought for free speech and tolerance.

pages.t: A pen that got him jailed
pages.x: François-Marie Arouet was born in Paris in 1694, the son of a lawyer, but he wanted to write. His mocking verses about the regent who ruled France got him locked in the Bastille for eleven months in 1717. There he wrote his first play and took the pen name Voltaire.

In 1726 a nobleman had his servants beat Voltaire with sticks after a quarrel. When Voltaire demanded a duel, he was thrown back into the Bastille, then sent into exile. In England he admired its free press, its tolerance, Newton and Shakespeare, and wrote a book praising them that was burned in Paris.

With a mathematician friend he spotted a flaw in the French state lottery: the prizes were worth more than all the tickets put together. They bought up the tickets and won a fortune, which kept him rich for the rest of his life.

In 1759 he published Candide, a short comic novel in which an innocent young man suffers war, earthquake, shipwreck and the Inquisition, while his tutor keeps insisting that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. It ends: "We must cultivate our garden."

From his estate at Ferney, near the Swiss border, he waged war on intolerance, signing his letters "Crush the infamous thing". He campaigned for years to clear the name of Jean Calas, a Protestant tortured and executed on a false charge, and won.

He is said to have drunk up to 50 cups of coffee a day, and he wrote more than 20,000 letters. Back in Paris at 83, he was crowned with laurels at a performance of one of his plays. He died a few weeks later, in 1778.

Voltaire was the leading voice of the Enlightenment, fighting for free speech, religious tolerance and reason. A later writer summed him up: "I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it."
pts: Champion of free speech and religious tolerance
The leading voice of the Enlightenment
